title: The Deuteronomistic History
aka: book of the law found in the temple
lead: Since Martin Noth (1943), most scholars have read Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings as one long history, written in Deuteronomy's language and judging Israel's kings by its laws. Others read these books as separate works, or see Deuteronomy as older and the source rather than the opening of that history.

sections.b: Martin Noth (1943) argued that Deuteronomy through 2 Kings, apart from Ruth, form one history, written in the exile to explain why Israel and Judah lost the land: they broke the covenant of Deuteronomy. Key speeches carry its message at turning points: Joshua's farewell (Joshua 23), Samuel's speech (1 Samuel 12), Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8) and the comment on the fall of Samaria (2 Kings 17:7–23). Kings are judged by Deuteronomy's standard of one place of worship, and Josiah, who finds the book of the law, is praised above all (2 Kings 23:25). Frank Moore Cross proposed a first edition under Josiah and a second in the exile; Rudolf Smend and others found several layers. Some recent scholars doubt there was ever one work. Traditional readers see the same unity as the result of later prophets writing in Deuteronomy's light.
